Newly settled juveniles of the Japanese sea cucumber Aspostichopus japonicus emerge from their planktonic larval stage at a remarkably small body size, with a total length at birth measuring just 0.2 cm [Lb = 0.2 cm]. The corresponding wet weight at this initial stage is only 0.001 grams [Wwb = 0.001 grams], reflecting the minimal biomass carried over from the auricularia larva through metamorphic climax. Under controlled rearing conditions maintained at a stable water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the transition from a bipinnaria-like auricularia to a settled juvenile occurs after approximately 10 days [ab = approximately 10 days], a duration that aligns with the rapid developmental pace observed in other temperate aspidochirotid holothuroids. This brief incubation period underscores the species' reliance on exogenous feeding soon after settlement to fuel the subsequent phase of somatic growth. The yolk-dependent embryo phase is correspondingly short, and the planktotrophic feeding onset of the auricularia larva must occur promptly to ensure adequate nutritional reserves for the allometric shift that defines larval metamorphosis.

During the post-metamorphic juvenile phase, individuals of A. japonicus undergo a period of accelerated somatic expansion before reaching the threshold that marks the onset of gonadal activation. Field surveys and laboratory growth trials indicate that puberty is attained when the individual reaches a total length of approximately 2 cm [Lp = approximately 2 cm], a size that correlates with a wet weight of roughly 0.2 grams [Wwp = roughly 0.2 grams]. The time required to achieve this developmental milestone from the moment of settlement has been documented under controlled thermal conditions; at a rearing temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the time since birth at puberty is approximately 90 days [tp = approximately 90 days]. This relatively rapid progression through the juvenile stage is typical of fast-growing echinoderms in productive coastal environments, where the energetic costs of tissue upkeep are offset by abundant food resources. The morphological transformation associated with the larval-juvenile transition is completed well before this point, allowing the growing juvenile to allocate resources predominantly to somatic expansion.

As individuals continue their ontogenetic trajectory, they eventually approach the asymptotic body dimensions characteristic of the species. Extensive surveys of natural populations in the Sea of Japan have established that the ultimate total length attained by A. japonicus reaches approximately 36.7 cm [Li = approximately 36.7 cm], a size that is accompanied by an ultimate wet weight of up to 1200 grams [Wwi = up to 1200 grams]. These maxima are generally achieved by sexually mature adults that have completed their primary somatic growth phase and have entered a period of sustained reproductive activity. The gravid adult echinoderms that attain these dimensions are typically found in sheltered bays with soft sediment substrates, where detrital food is abundant enough to support such substantial biomass. Comparisons with congeneric species from higher latitudes suggest that the asymptotic size of A. japonicus is near the upper end of the range for its genus, possibly reflecting the relatively long growing season in its temperate habitat. The reproductively active adults that reach these sizes commonly exhibit robust gonad development and participate in annual spawning events.

Longevity data for A. japonicus, derived from both mark-recapture studies and size-frequency analysis, indicate that the species exhibits a moderate lifespan relative to other holothuroids. The maximum lifespan in the wild has been estimated at approximately 7 years [am = approximately 7 years], based on observations of individuals maintained in environments where the ambient water temperature averages 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This duration is consistent with the life-history strategies of many temperate deposit-feeding echinoderms that experience seasonal fluctuations in food availability. The onset of reproductive senescence typically occurs only in the oldest individuals, with most adults remaining capable of spawning for several consecutive years. The physiological processes that ultimately lead to natural mortality are thought to involve a progressive deterioration of organ function rather than a single catastrophic event.

The reproductive biology of A. japonicus is characterized by a single annual spawning event, a pattern common among temperate aspidochirotid sea cucumbers. Females produce a substantial number of oocytes, with a typical fecundity per reproductive event of approximately 3,000,000 eggs per spawning [N_R_i = approximately 3,000,000 eggs per spawning]. Given that spawning occurs once per year [F_R_i = spawning occurs once per year], the daily reproduction rate is implicit in this annual cycle. The timing of this first spawning event is critical for population replenishment; the age at first reproduction has been recorded at approximately 2 years after birth [tR = approximately 2 years after birth]. The chemotaxis-guided fertilisation that follows gamete broadcast ensures high fertilisation success when adult densities are adequate. This reproductive strategy, combining a single, high-fecundity annual event with external fertilisation in the water column, is well suited to the stable, food-rich coastal environments where Japanese sea cucumbers are most abundant.
